sources.entry: Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time - Decides how many builds, runs and iterations an experiment needs by measuring at which level the variation arises.

summary.title: Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time
summary.one_liner: You learn a statistically rigorous, cost-aware method for deciding how many builds, VM invocations and benchmark iterations an experiment needs, and how to report results with effect size confidence intervals.
takeaways: Repetition should be allocated at the level where most variation arises: builds, executions (VM invocations) or iterations.
A mathematical cost model identifies the necessary and sufficient number of repetitions at each level for a target precision.
The paper gives a cookbook for choosing repetition counts so results are reliable without excessive experiment time.
Results should be presented with an effect size confidence interval rather than a bare difference.
The method is demonstrated with throughput experiments using DaCapo and SPEC CPU benchmarks on three recent platforms.
summary.summary: The paper argues that many systems evaluations under-repeat experiments and report results without proper variation estimates, making small differences unreliable. It proposes a statistically rigorous methodology that models experimentation cost and uses the observation that most non-determinism in a given benchmark on a given platform is smaller than worst-case studies suggest, and that repetition should target the level where uncertainty mainly arises. The authors present the approach as a cookbook for choosing repetition counts at each experiment level and for reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals. They illustrate it with throughput experiments using DaCapo and SPEC CPU on three recent platforms. The page is the repository record for the ISMM 2013 paper, and the abstract notes this version corrects the original.
